newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German 1997 tax estimates.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German 1997 tax estimates.

text.p: The German finance ministry said on Thursday that estimates for 1997 tax revenues showed an 18.0 billion mark shortfall.
Following is a selection of economists' reactions to the news.
HOLGER SCHMIEDING, MERRILL LYNCH IN FRANKFURT

"This is a big budget problem, but it is pretty much a problem that we already knew about. On top of this, of course, the federal government will have extra outlays for unemployment which could be another six billion marks on the expenditure side. We have quite a bit to do to meet the Maastricht criteria, and it looks like we will not make it."

"The figure is broadly in line with expectations, but we feel that it is highly damaging for the credibility of the government that it is apparently seeking to revalue the Bundesbank's gold assets to get a handle on its problems with the deficit ratio to qualify for the Maastricht criteria.
"This is the not at all what the Bundesbank and the government itself have called for from other countries. They called against one-off measures and for sustainable consolidation of public finances."

"The numbers were actually in line with expectations. If you consider that Waigel had already budgeted for an 8.0 billion mark shortfall and now he has 18 billion marks then he has got some 10 billion marks that are uncovered on the spending side. But in total the deficit will still be 20 billion marks higher considering the high unemployment rate.
"Germany will certainly not make the 3.0 percent deficit criterion and at some point, he (Waigel) will have to eat his words and say that a number slightly above three percent will be fine too."
RUTGER TEUSCHER, DEUTSCHE BANK RESEARCH IN FRANKFURT

"It is questionable whether we will get an indirect tax hike, such as mineral oil tax hike. But the overall tax shortfall is too huge to be tackled without such a measure, unless there are some other decisive spending cuts, not only by the federal government but also by the federal states.
"A spending freeze now seems unavoidable -- such a measure could bring in two or three billion marks on the federal side."
